# SQLite session extension, changesets, patchsets, and `sqldiff`

Everything below was read from the SQLite source tree on GitHub (`sqlite/sqlite`, `master`,
fetched 2026-09-14). `sqlite.org` itself is blocked by this session's egress proxy, so the
authoritative doc comments in `ext/session/sqlite3session.h` and `ext/session/sqlite3session.c`
stand in for the published pages (they are the same text the website renders).

Sources:
- [`ext/session/sqlite3session.h`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sqlite/sqlite/master/ext/session/sqlite3session.h)
  — the public API doc comments (what the website's `session.html` pages are generated from).
- [`ext/session/sqlite3session.c`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sqlite/sqlite/master/ext/session/sqlite3session.c)
  — the binary `CHANGESET FORMAT` / `PATCHSET FORMAT` block comments, lines ~197-280.
- [`tool/sqldiff.c`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sqlite/sqlite/master/tool/sqldiff.c)

## 1. What a changeset is

> "A changeset consists of zero or more INSERT, UPDATE and/or DELETE changes, each representing a
> change to a single row of an attached table. An INSERT change contains the values of each field
> of a new database row. A DELETE contains the original values of each field of a deleted database
> row. An UPDATE change contains the original values of each field of an updated database row along
> with the updated values for each updated non-primary-key column."
> — `sqlite3session.h`, `sqlite3session_changeset()`

**It is a net diff, not a log.** This is stated explicitly:

> "This means, amongst other things, that if a row is inserted and then later deleted while a
> session object is active, neither the insert nor the delete will be present in the changeset. Or
> if a row is deleted and then later a row with the same primary key values inserted while a
> session object is active, the resulting changeset will contain an UPDATE change instead of a
> DELETE and an INSERT."

The mechanism is worth knowing because it explains the edge cases: the session object only
accumulates, per unique primary key, *the first* record of a touched row ("For each unique primary
key value, data is only recorded once — the first time a row with said primary key is inserted,
updated or deleted in the lifetime of the session"). At `sqlite3session_changeset()` time it joins
those accumulated keys against **the live database** and emits INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE / nothing
accordingly. A row updated back to its original values produces no change at all:

> "If there is a row with a matching primary key in the database, but all fields contain their
> original values, no change is added to the changeset."

## 2. What an UPDATE actually carries — the important gotcha

The wire format comment is blunter than the API doc:

> "Within the old.* record associated with an UPDATE change, all fields associated with table
> columns that are not PRIMARY KEY columns and are not modified by the UPDATE change are set to
> "undefined". Other fields are set to the values that made up the row before the UPDATE that the
> change records took place. Within the new.* record, fields associated with table columns modified
> by the UPDATE change contain the new values. Fields associated with table columns that are not
> modified are set to "undefined"."
> — `sqlite3session.c`, `CHANGESET FORMAT`

So an UPDATE change is **PK + changed-columns-only, on both sides**. It is *not* a before-row and
an after-row. A consumer cannot read the value of an unchanged column out of a changeset at all —
neither before nor after. (Seahaven's `src/seahaven/changes.py` already models this correctly: it
drops `apsw.no_change` cells, and its `Change` docstring says so. But any judge written against
`before`/`after` must expect columns to be *absent*, and must go to live state — `run_sql` or the
tables themselves — to read an unchanged column.)

INSERT and DELETE are whole rows: "In the changeset format, the records that are part of INSERT or
DELETE changes never contain any undefined (type byte 0x00) fields."

## 3. Ordering is undefined

Verbatim from `sqlite3session.h`:

> "Within a changeset generated by this function, all changes related to a single table are grouped
> together. In other words, when iterating through a changeset or when applying a changeset to a
> database, all changes related to a single table are processed before moving on to the next table.
> Tables are sorted in the same order in which they were attached (or auto-attached) to the
> sqlite3_session object. **The order in which the changes related to a single table are stored is
> undefined.**"

And the format comment agrees: "Operations on a single table are grouped together, but may occur in
any order (i.e. deletes, updates and inserts are all mixed together)."

Reading the implementation (`sessionGenerateChangeset`, `sqlite3session.c` ~line 3143) confirms
*why*: it walks the per-table hash table `pTab->apChange[0..nChange)` and, within each bucket, the
`pNext` chain. That is hash-bucket order over the primary key, with a bucket count that grows as
more rows are touched (`sessionGrowHash`) — **not** rowid order, not PK order, not write order.

> ⚠️ Seahaven's `changes.py` `render()` docstring currently asserts: *"That order is by table and
> then by rowid, which is deterministic for a given sequence of writes, so two identical runs render
> identically."* The first clause is not what the source says. The determinism conclusion is
> probably still true in practice for an identical sequence of writes against an identical build
> (the hash is a pure function of the PK bytes, and the bucket count a function of how many rows
> were touched), but it is an undocumented implementation detail that SQLite explicitly reserves the
> right to change. If a judge or a golden file depends on order, sort it yourself.

## 4. How rows are identified

By the **declared** PRIMARY KEY, and only that:

> "Changes can only be recorded for tables that have a PRIMARY KEY explicitly defined as part of
> their CREATE TABLE statement."

> "It is not an error if the named table does not exist in the database. Nor is it an error if the
> named table does not have a PRIMARY KEY. However, no changes will be recorded in either of these
> scenarios."

That silent-no-op is the trap Seahaven's `_refuse_a_table_with_no_primary_key()` guards against.

Two further silent-loss cases, both verbatim:

- "Changes are not recorded for rows that have NULL values stored in one or more of their PRIMARY
  KEY columns."  With the follow-on: a row updated *out of* a NULL PK appears as an INSERT only; a
  row updated *into* a NULL PK appears as a DELETE only.
- "It is not possible for an UPDATE change to represent a change that modifies the values of primary
  key columns. If such a change is made, it is represented in a changeset as a DELETE followed by an
  INSERT."  **A judge that counts `op == "update"` will miss PK rewrites.**

### `SQLITE_SESSION_OBJCONFIG_ROWID` — tracking PK-less tables

There *is* an escape hatch, added later than most session docs suggest:

> "This option is used to set, clear or query the flag that enables collection of data for tables
> with no explicit PRIMARY KEY. Normally, tables with no explicit PRIMARY KEY are simply ignored by
> the sessions module. However, if this flag is set, it behaves as if such tables have a column
> `_rowid_ INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` inserted as their leftmost columns. It is an error (SQLITE_MISUSE) to
> attempt to modify this setting after the first table has been attached to the session object."

I bisected the SQLite GitHub mirror's release tags for the symbol `SQLITE_SESSION_OBJCONFIG_ROWID`:
absent at `version-3.40.0` and `version-3.41.0`, present at `version-3.42.0` and later. So it is a
**3.42.0 (2023-05) or later** feature. Caveat: the mirror tags are what I tested, not an official
changelog entry — sqlite.org's release notes are unreachable from this session.

Note the shape change it implies: with the flag on, the changeset's column list gains a synthetic
leftmost `_rowid_` column, so the rendered `key`/`before`/`after` for such a table would carry a
rowid that is *not* a user-visible column and is not stable across a vacuum/reload.

## 5. Patchsets

> "The differences between a patchset and a changeset are that: DELETE records consist of the
> primary key fields only. The original values of other fields are omitted. The original values of
> any modified fields are omitted from UPDATE records."

So a patchset is strictly *less* informative: DELETE loses the deleted row's contents; UPDATE loses
the old values. Consequences stated in the source: no `SQLITE_CHANGESET_DATA` conflicts can be
detected when applying one, and `sqlite3changeset_invert()` "returns SQLITE_CORRUPT if it is passed
a patchset". For grading, a patchset is the wrong choice — "what did this row look like before" is
exactly the question a judge asks.

Format-level: a changeset table header starts with byte `0x54` ('T'), a patchset with `0x50` ('P'),
so the two are self-identifying.

## 6. Conflict vocabulary (useful as a source of names, not as a judge API)

From `sqlite3changeset_apply()`: `SQLITE_CHANGESET_DATA` (row present but "before" values differ),
`SQLITE_CHANGESET_NOTFOUND` (row absent), `SQLITE_CHANGESET_CONFLICT` (INSERT would duplicate a PK),
`SQLITE_CHANGESET_CONSTRAINT` (UNIQUE/CHECK/NOT NULL), `SQLITE_CHANGESET_FOREIGN_KEY` (invoked
"exactly once before the changeset is committed").

## 7. Other pieces of the session extension worth knowing

- **Indirect changes.** Every change carries a 1-byte indirect flag. "A change is marked as indirect
  if either: the session object "indirect" flag is set when the change is made, or the change is
  made by an SQL trigger or foreign key action instead of directly as a result of a users SQL
  statement." Seahaven's renderer currently discards this. It is the only built-in signal that
  distinguishes "the agent wrote this" from "a trigger/audit-row wrote this", which is precisely the
  "irrelevant changes" problem the research plan flags for benchmarks. Available via
  `sqlite3changeset_op(..., int *pbIndirect)`.
- **Changegroups** (`sqlite3changegroup_*`) concatenate/coalesce several changesets into one net
  changeset — the way to fold per-step changesets into an episode-level diff if you ever record per
  step.
- **Size accounting** is opt-in: `SQLITE_SESSION_OBJCONFIG_SIZE` enables
  `sqlite3session_changeset_size()`, and is "disabled by default" because "it imposes some
  computational overhead". Relevant if you want to bound how big a state payload can get.

## 8. `sqldiff` — the two-database variant

`tool/sqldiff.c` is a separate utility: "This is a utility program that computes the differences in
content between two SQLite databases." Its help text:

```
Usage: sqldiff [options] DB1 DB2
Output SQL text that would transform DB1 into DB2.
Options:
  --changeset FILE      Write a CHANGESET into FILE
  -L|--lib LIBRARY      Load an SQLite extension library
  --primarykey          Use schema-defined PRIMARY KEYs
  --rbu                 Output SQL to create/populate RBU table(s)
  --schema              Show only differences in the schema
  --summary             Show only a summary of the differences
  --table TAB           Show only differences in table TAB
  --transaction         Show SQL output inside a transaction
  --vtab                Handle fts3, fts4, fts5 and rtree tables
```

Key differences from the session extension:

| | session changeset | `sqldiff` |
|---|---|---|
| Input | a live connection, instrumented *before* the writes | two finished database files |
| Default row key | declared PRIMARY KEY only (PK-less tables ignored) | the *true* primary key — "the rowid or INTEGER PRIMARY KEY for ordinary tables or the declared PRIMARY KEY for WITHOUT ROWID tables"; `--primarykey` switches to the schema-declared PK |
| Output | binary blob (needs an iterator) | SQL text (`UPDATE`/`INSERT`/`DELETE` statements), or a changeset with `--changeset` |
| Schema changes | not represented | emitted as DDL |
| Needs a baseline copy? | no | yes — you must keep the fixture database around |

The emitted UPDATE statements carry **only changed columns** (`sqldiff.c` ~line 675: it skips a
column when the per-column "changed" flag is 0, then appends `WHERE pk=...`). DELETE is keyed on the
PK only; INSERT lists every column. So the information content is close to a patchset, and the
output is SQL text — the least machine-queryable of any format surveyed here.

Because it works on two files, `sqldiff` is the fallback when you did *not* instrument the run
(e.g. grading an episode from a saved snapshot pair), and it is the only one of the two that can
diff schema. It also has the appealing property that it needs no cooperation from the world at
write time.
